scenes.name: Black Sabbath
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: Con Led Zeppelin, la banda fundadora del heavy según la mayoría (los británicos la prefieren a ella). Se llamaban Earth, un nombre hippie, hasta que una confusión con una banda de cabaret los mandó a tocar a una fiesta que esperaba valses; adoptaron el título de una película de terror de Boris Karloff, que ya era el de una de sus canciones, como corrección expresa del «paz y amor». Geezer Butler cuenta que un crítico americano describió su música hacia 1972 como «el sonido del heavy metal estrellándose». Su gira se anunciaba como «más ruidosa que Led Zeppelin»; abrían para ellos Yes, Alice Cooper o los Ramones. Su tema más famoso sobre drogas, «Sweet Leaf», es más psicodélico que heavy; «Iron Man» es uno de los monstruos favoritos del metal y «Children of the Grave», una canción contra la guerra atómica.

scenes.name: La «muerte» del metal en los noventa
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: A mediados de los noventa se expide el certificado de defunción del metal, y hay varios sospechosos. Para los headbangers fue una puñalada de Metallica: el disco homónimo de 1991, lleno de baladas radiables, Load y ReLoad, el cartel de Lollapalooza y la portada de Rolling Stone con pelo corto, eyeliner y piercings. Otros culpan al grunge, que destrona al lite metal justo cuando Skid Row, Mötley Crüe, Van Halen y Guns N’ Roses debutaban en el número uno en 1991. Pero los grandes grupos también se oxidan: Black Sabbath lleva quince años de cambios de cantante (Dehumanizer con Dio en 1992 y luego solo queda Tony Iommi), Ozzy anuncia que se retira y se desretira, Judas Priest queda inerte tras Painkiller cuando Halford se marcha a Fight y lo ven como un Judas, Bruce Dickinson deja Iron Maiden en 1993. Los fans se consuelan con bandas tributo y discos de homenaje (Nativity in Black, 1994), y el último clavo del ataúd es el disco de versiones melódicas de Pat Boone, In a Metal Mood.

podcast.title: Factory Accident and Finger Injury (1966)
podcast.body: At age 17, while working in a Birmingham factory that manufactured metal rings, Iommi suffered an industrial accident on his last day of work. Reassigned to a huge press that operated like a guillotine due to a colleague's absence, his right hand was caught, severing the ends of his middle and ring fingers. Doctors informed him he might as well forget about playing the guitar. "bang, it came down. It just took the ends off my fingers. I actually pulled them off."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: DIY Prosthetic Thimbles
podcast.body: To manage the pain and difficulty of playing guitar after his injury, Iommi fashioned plastic thimbles from a dishwashing soap bottle and wrapped them in leather from an old jacket. These thimbles allowed him to play but made it difficult to feel the strings, requiring him to press down very hard. "he fashioned a couple of plastic thimbles from a bottle of dishwashing soap and wrapped them in leather from an old leather jacket."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Development of Signature Sound
podcast.body: Due to his finger injury and the use of thimbles, Iommi found soloing tough and concentrated on playing heavy power chords. He couldn't bend standard guitar strings well, so he used banjo strings and tuned his guitar low to C sharp (drop C sharp) to make them looser and easier to play. This combination of techniques—heavy power chords, banjo strings, and low tuning—created the distinctive heavy, sinister, and powerful guitar sound that made Black Sabbath famous and significantly contributed to the sound of heavy metal. "Put this all together, and you have the distinctive guitar sound that made his band, Black Sabbath, famous."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Factory Accident and Finger Loss
podcast.body: The day before Tony Iommi was scheduled to quit his factory job to pursue Black Sabbath full-time, he suffered a severe accident where sheet metal sliced off a couple of his fingertips. This industrial injury fundamentally altered his guitar playing technique and, consequently, the sound of his music. "The day before he was going to quit his job at a factory to go with the band full time, some sheet metal sliced off a couple of fingertips."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Grunge
podcast.body: More than a decade after Black Sabbath's rise, a new generation of metal-adjacent bands from the Pacific Northwest, influenced by Tony Iommi, adopted his "no fingers tuning," specifically drop D or drop C sharp. This tuning became a foundational element of the grunge genre. "That dropped D or in Tony's case, drop C sharp became the foundation of grunge."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Innovative Playing Solution
podcast.body: To continue playing after his accident, Iommi created his own prosthetics by melting plastic and lining them with leather. However, playing with these was difficult and painful. To make it more comfortable, he switched to thinner strings and reduced their tension, which naturally resulted in a lower tuning. This painful solution led directly to a dark, slow, and almost tenebrous sound that defined his band. "Para poder seguir tocando, se fabrica unas protechis, fundiendo plástico y forrándolas con cuero, pero la resulta complicado y doloroso tocar con ellas. Para que les sea más cómodo, cambia las cuerdas por una más finas y reduce su tensión, logrando si una finación más grave."

srcs.episode: El DOOM METAL es el DARK SOULS de la música

podcast.title: Inspiration from Django Reinhart
podcast.body: After his factory accident, Iommi's foreman, feeling sympathetic, played him a recording by guitarist Django Reinhart. Reinhart, despite terrible burns to his hand leaving him with only two workable fingers, became a master of the guitar, inspiring Iommi to continue playing despite his own injury. "That inspired Tony to keep going, but it was painful."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Work Accident and Injury (Age 17)
podcast.body: At just 17 years old, while working in Birmingham, Tony Iommi suffered an industrial accident with a metal cutting machine that severed two phalanges from his right hand. This was his fretting hand, crucial for playing the guitar. "Con tan solo 17 años, Tony Ayomi, un joven guitarrista de Birmingham, en la terra, acaba de tener un accidente laboral con un acordador a metal que le ha reban a dos falanges de su mano derecha, justo la mano con la que controlan los trascés."

awards.title: Order of the Badge of Honour

xref.title: Creation of Heavy Metal Sound
xref.body: The distinctive guitar sound of Black Sabbath, characterized by its heaviness, sinister quality, and power, was largely a result of Tony Iommi's adaptations after a factory accident. His use of plastic thimbles, banjo strings, and a low C sharp tuning allowed him to play despite his injury and became fundamental to the band's influential sound, which is credited with shaping heavy metal as it is known today. "And the Sabbath sound went a long way to creating the sound of heavy metal as we know it today."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on Tom Morello
xref.body: Tom Morello extensively studied old Black Sabbath records, specifically noting how guitarist Tony Iommi demonstrated restraint and utilized the importance of the "space between the notes" in his playing. "He also spent a lot of time listening to old black Sabbath records, noting how guitarist Tony Iomey often exhibited restraint, utilizing that the space between the notes could be as important as the notes themselves."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Overcoming Injury to Master Guitar
xref.body: Django Reinhart was a guitarist who suffered severe burns to his hand, leaving him with only two workable fingers. Despite this debilitating injury, he managed to become a master of the guitar, serving as an inspiration to Tony Iommi after Iommi's own hand accident. "Reinhart had suffered terrible burns to his hand, leaving him with just two workable fingers, yet he became a master of the guitar."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Tony Iommi's Influence on Restraint
xref.body: He studied old Black Sabbath records to observe how Tony Iommi effectively used restraint, recognizing the importance of the "space between the notes" in his playing. "He also spent a lot of time listening to old black Sabbath records, noting how guitarist Tony Iomey often exhibited restraint, utilizing that the space between the notes could be as important as the notes themselves."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
